heard: The most famous star in the sky ranks 48th in brightness. Millions of sky watchers mistakenly believe Polaris is the brightest star above Earth. In reality, Sirius blazes roughly 25 times brighter because it sits only 8.7 light years away. Polaris sits over 430 light years away, though it is intrinsically thousands of times more luminous than our sun. Navigators rely on Polaris solely because it aligns almost directly above Earth's northern rotational axis. But Earth wobbles on its rotational axis over a 26,000-year cycle called precession. Around the year 2100, Polaris reaches its closest northern alignment before slowly drifting away. In 13,000 years, the brilliant star Vega will take over as our new north star. Until then, many will still falsely assume that the north star is the brightest.
